shape: A bright, round, flat light that changed from white to reddish-orange, with tongues of red, yellow and green light
witnesses: Patrolman Robert Dickerson of the Redmond police; FAA flight service specialists at the airport
duration: Minutes in sight; the radar reports lasted about two hours
summary: Before dawn on September 24, 1959, a Redmond police officer, Robert Dickerson, saw what he first took for a falling meteor stop and hover a few hundred feet up north of the airport. FAA staff at the Redmond flight service station watched it move off to the north-east, project “long tongues of red, yellow and green light”, and, when a fast aircraft approached, rise into the clouds, then reappear to the south. The station reported it to Seattle Air Route Traffic Control Center at 1310 GMT; Seattle’s log said the Klamath Falls ground-controlled intercept radar had it, and F-102s were scrambled from Portland. Seattle later passed on radar reports of an object 25 miles from Redmond at altitudes up to 52,000 ft. The FAA’s logged account, sent to NICAP, made the case famous; the Air Force’s answers changed from a balloon to insufficient data to Venus, and in 1960 Blue Book concluded that the light was Venus and that no radar track had been confirmed.

title: Red Bluff — California Highway Patrol sighting
place: Red Bluff area, Tehama County, California
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The Air Force concluded the Red Bluff sightings were due to atmospheric refraction, most probably of the planet Mars rising, with a strong temperature inversion and a layer of forest-fire smoke adding to the effect.
shape: Football-shaped object with red lights at each end
witnesses: CHP officers Charles Carson and Stanley Scott; sheriff's deputies
summary: Two California Highway Patrol officers thought they were about to see an airliner crash when a large object dropped toward the road ahead of them. At about 100–200 ft it stopped, reversed and climbed. They watched it for more than two hours as it moved about the sky, swept a red beam over the area and caused radio interference. Deputies at the Tehama County sheriff's office also saw lights. Similar reports came from across northern California that week.

title: Betty and Barney Hill
place: U.S. Route 3, Franconia Notch to Indian Head, New Hampshire
explanation: The Air Force file notes that Jupiter was low in the south-west and would have set about when the object disappeared, and that there was a strong temperature inversion. The abduction story emerged only under hypnosis in 1964. The psychiatrist, Dr. Benjamin Simon, believed it was a fantasy that grew out of Betty's dreams.
shape: Pancake-shaped craft with windows and lights
witnesses: 2 (Betty and Barney Hill)
duration: Sighting ~1 hour; about 2 hours unaccounted for
summary: Driving home to Portsmouth from Montreal, the Hills saw a light moving near the Moon south of Lancaster. It followed them through Franconia Notch, passing near the Cannon Mountain tramway. South of Indian Head it came down to about 100 ft over the road, and Barney saw figures at the windows through binoculars. They reached home around dawn, about two hours later than expected. Under hypnosis in 1964 both described being taken aboard, in the first widely publicised "alien abduction".

title: Bahía Blanca and Espora air base sightings
place: Bahía Blanca and Espora Naval Air Base
shape: Lighted "railroad car"; ball of light
witnesses: Base personnel, truck drivers, a newspaper photographer
summary: In May 1962 objects were reported at the Espora naval air base on May 11 and 18. On May 12, three truck drivers on Route 35 said an illuminated object like a railway carriage rose from a field, crossed the road at about 4 m and split in two. On May 21, La Nueva Provincia photographer Miguel Tohmé photographed an object over the city, and the photo made the front page. Sightings at the Puerto Belgrano naval base followed.

title: Trancas — lights over the Moreno farm
place: Finca of the Moreno family beside the Belgrano railway, Trancas, Tucumán
shape: Several luminous objects, some over the railway line and one near the gate; a beam of light that turned violet
witnesses: The sisters Argentina and Yolie Moreno, the house worker Dora Martínez Guzmán, and others in the household
summary: At about 10 p.m. on October 21, 1963, the women of the Moreno family at their farm near Trancas, in Tucumán, saw several bright lights over the Belgrano railway line beside the property and one close to the gate. A beam from one was turned on them; it changed from white to violet, surrounded by a fog, and they felt intense heat. Figures seemed to move around the lights on the tracks. After about forty minutes the lights left in formation towards the Medina hills. The police report described a white mist with a strong smell of sulphur lasting forty minutes, and small white balls and a powder found by the tracks were later analysed as mostly calcium carbonate. The case was widely reported at the time and is one of the classic Argentine close encounters. Later local accounts add burns to the worker’s face and arm and bare ground where nothing grew; these are not in the contemporary record. La Gaceta notes that soldiers from Tucumán regiments were being moved along those tracks for exercises at the time, which could account for figures seen walking there; nobody has explained the lights.

title: Socorro landing (Lonnie Zamora)
explanation: Project Blue Book listed the case as "unknown" — one of its best-known. Proposed explanations include a lunar-lander test and a student hoax; none is confirmed.
shape: Shiny egg / "O" shape on legs; red insignia
witnesses: Police Sgt. Lonnie Zamora
summary: Chasing a speeder south of Socorro, Sgt. Lonnie Zamora heard a roar and saw flame, drove toward it and saw a whitish oval object in a gully with two small figures in white beside it. The object rose on a blue-orange flame and left. Investigators found scorched brush and four depressions.

title: The Solway Firth “spaceman” photograph
place: Burgh Marsh, near Burgh by Sands, Cumberland
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: In 2014 the researcher David Clarke concluded that the “spaceman” is most likely Templeton’s wife, Annie, who was there that day: seen from behind, her pale blue dress overexposed to white, standing beyond what the camera’s viewfinder showed. Darkened and straightened, the figure looks like a person seen from the back.
shape: A tall white figure in what looks like a space suit and helmet, behind the child
witnesses: Jim Templeton, a Carlisle fireman and photographer, his wife and their five-year-old daughter
duration: One photograph in a sequence of three
summary: On May 23, 1964, Jim Templeton photographed his five-year-old daughter Elizabeth sitting on Burgh Marsh, overlooking the Solway Firth. He said that no one else was in sight, but when the film came back the middle of three frames showed a tall white figure apparently in a space suit standing behind her. Kodak said the picture had not been tampered with, the Carlisle police found nothing suspicious, and the photograph went round the world. Templeton later told of two men claiming to be from the government who quizzed him at the marsh, and repeated a story that a Blue Streak launch at Woomera had been stopped by two similar figures. In 2014 David Clarke proposed the explanation now generally given: Templeton’s wife had walked into the background, her back to the camera, outside the part of the scene the viewfinder showed, and the overexposed blue dress turned white.

title: Big Sur — Atlas "Buzzing Bee" film
place: Anderson Peak, Big Sur, and Vandenberg AFB, California
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Project engineer Kingston George wrote in 1993 that the film showed the re-entry vehicle releasing decoy warheads and chaff, a classified technology at the time, which Jacobs was not cleared to know about.
shape: Object circling a missile warhead
witnesses: 1369th Photographic Squadron team
summary: In 1964 an Air Force team on Anderson Peak used a telescope borrowed from Boston University to film Atlas missile launches from Vandenberg. In 1982, Robert Jacobs, the officer in charge on the mountain, said the film of one launch, nicknamed "Buzzing Bee", showed an object fly around the warhead and hit it with beams of light, and that the film had been confiscated. The project engineer said it showed decoy deployment.

title: Valensole landing
explanation: Investigated by the Gendarmerie; the ground marks and the effect on lavender plants were documented but never explained.
shape: Egg-shaped craft on legs; two small beings
witnesses: Farmer Maurice Masse
summary: Lavender farmer Maurice Masse said he found a rugby-ball-shaped craft on six legs in his field and two small beings beside it; one pointed a tube at him and he was paralysed. The craft left marks in the soil where lavender failed to grow for years.

title: Deception Island — the Antarctic sightings
place: Argentine station, Deception Island, South Shetland Islands
explanation: The Argentine Navy said in an official statement that its observers had seen a solid, lens-shaped flying object, and Lt. Daniel Perisse, at the Argentine station, said a weather balloon, a plane or a star had been ruled out. No explanation was ever published, and the photographs said to have been taken have not been released.
shape: Lens-shaped object, mostly red and green, changing to yellow, blue, white and orange
witnesses: Seventeen people at the Argentine station; nine at the Chilean station; five at the British base; two meteorologists on Laurie Island
summary: Over two winter nights in July 1965, the staff of three stations on Deception Island and of the Argentine station on Laurie Island, in the South Orkneys, reported a coloured, manoeuvring light. On July 2 five British observers saw a green and red light zig-zag, hover and speed up. On the evening of July 3, nine Chilean observers watched a light change colour and leave a steam-like trail, and at 19:42 seventeen people at the Argentine station, three Chilean visitors among them, watched a lens-shaped object. In a statement on July 6, the Argentine Navy described “a giant, lens-shaped flying object, solid in appearance, mostly red and green in color”, moving on a zig-zag course toward the east with changes of speed and direction, without sound, 10 to 15 km away. On Laurie Island, two variometers registered “sudden and strong disturbances of the magnetic field” during a 15-second sighting.

title: Buenos Aires — Meteors scrambled
shape: Two bright discs
witnesses: Many residents; Argentine Air Force
summary: Two bright discs hung motionless over Buenos Aires for about ten minutes, then flew off at high speed. With calls pouring in, the Seventh Air Brigade scrambled three Gloster Meteor jets from Morón air base, which found nothing.

title: August 1965 — lights over Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas
place: Oklahoma City and across Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas and New Mexico
explanation: The Air Force first suggested a meteor shower, then said the lights were stars and planets made to change colour by scintillation, naming Jupiter among them. Planetarium directors in Oklahoma objected that Jupiter was not in the evening sky at that season; one suggested Antares or Vega. The reported radar contacts were never confirmed: a Tinker AFB spokesman would neither confirm nor deny them, and the base’s approach-control radar reported no contacts at the peak.
shape: Coloured lights, red, white and blue-green, reported hovering and moving
witnesses: Oklahoma Highway Patrol and police officers, weather observers and thousands of residents
duration: From about 8 p.m. to 3 a.m., and again the following nights
summary: On the night of August 1, 1965, from about 8 p.m. until 3 a.m., a steady stream of reports came in from Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas and New Mexico of coloured lights moving in the sky, some in formation. The Oklahoma Highway Patrol said officers in several towns had seen them and that Tinker Air Force Base had as many as four on radar at once at about 22,000 ft. Tinker would neither confirm nor deny the radar contacts, and its approach-control radar reported none during the height of the local sightings. The reports continued for several nights, and Blue Book received dozens from the region. The Air Force answered first that people were seeing the Delta Aquarid meteors, then that they were seeing bright stars and planets, which led to public objections from planetarium staff that the planets named were not in view.

title: Heflin Polaroids — Santa Ana
place: Myford Road near Santa Ana, California
explanation: Project Blue Book classed the photographs as a hoax. Analysts argued the "UFO" was a small object hung or thrown near the van. Supporters point out that Heflin's originals were never shown to be faked.
shape: Hat-shaped disc; a smoke ring
witnesses: 1 (Rex Heflin, highway traffic investigator)
summary: Orange County highway traffic investigator Rex Heflin was photographing road signs from his work van when he saw a hat-shaped object cross the road ahead. He took three Polaroid pictures through the windshield and side window, then a fourth of a smoke ring it seemed to leave behind. The photos were printed in the Santa Ana Register and studied by the Air Force and the Condon Committee.

title: Incident at Exeter
explanation: The Air Force first blamed a military exercise and twinkling stars, then changed the case to "unidentified". A 2011 Skeptical Inquirer analysis proposed a KC-97 refuelling tanker.
shape: Row of five pulsing red lights
witnesses: Norman Muscarello; officers Bertrand and Hunt
summary: Hitchhiker Norman Muscarello saw five pulsing red lights hover over a field on Route 150 and rushed to the Exeter police station. Returning with Officer Eugene Bertrand, both — and then Officer David Hunt — watched the lights rise from behind trees and move over the field.

title: Kecksburg fireball
explanation: Astronomers identified a bright bolide seen from six states and Ontario; no object was found at Kecksburg. Claims of a recovered acorn-shaped craft are unsupported, and the Soviet Kosmos 96 re-entry was ruled out by timing.
shape: Fireball; later claims of an acorn-shaped object
witnesses: Thousands across six states
summary: A brilliant fireball crossed the sky over the Detroit–Windsor area and was reported from Ontario to Pennsylvania. Residents of Kecksburg said something fell into the woods; state police and military personnel searched and reported finding nothing.

title: Tully "saucer nest"
explanation: Police and the RAAF suggested a willy-willy (whirlwind) flattened the reeds; others considered it unexplained.
shape: Grey saucer rising from the lagoon
witnesses: Banana grower George Pedley
summary: George Pedley heard a hissing sound and saw a saucer-shaped object rise from a lagoon and climb away. In its place was a floating circle of flattened, clockwise-swirled reeds about 9 m across — the original "saucer nest".

title: Michigan "swamp gas" sightings
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: J. Allen Hynek, the Air Force's scientific consultant, suggested that burning marsh gas might explain some of the lights over the swamps, and Blue Book filed the flap as "marsh gas". The explanation was widely ridiculed. Hynek later said he regretted how it was presented.
shape: Football-shaped object with lights; glowing lights over a swamp
witnesses: Farm family, a dozen police officers, 87 college students
summary: On March 20, 1966, Frank Mannor and his son near Dexter said they walked toward a glowing, football-shaped object hovering over a swamp. About a dozen police officers reported lights. The next night 87 women at Hillsdale College watched a light hover over the campus arboretum for hours. Congressman Gerald Ford called for hearings, which led to the Condon Committee.

title: Westall school sighting
place: Westall High School, Clayton South, Melbourne
explanation: Researchers have proposed a stray HIBAL cosmic-ray research balloon launched from Mildura, trailed by light aircraft.
shape: Silvery disc; descended into a paddock
witnesses: 200+ students and teachers
summary: Students and staff watched a silvery disc descend behind trees into a paddock known as The Grange, then rise and leave while light aircraft circled. Several students said they saw a flattened circle in the grass.

title: Portage County police chase
explanation: Project Blue Book (Maj. Hector Quintanilla) concluded the officers first saw the Echo satellite and then Venus; the officers and Rep. William Stanton rejected this.
shape: Bright disc-shaped light, "as big as a house"
witnesses: Deputies Dale Spaur & Wilbur Neff, officers in three towns
summary: Portage County sheriff’s deputies Dale Spaur and Wilbur Neff, checking an abandoned car on Route 224, saw a brilliantly lit object rise from the woods. Told by radio to follow it, they chased it east at up to 100 mph for about 85 miles into Pennsylvania, joined by officers from East Palestine and Conway, PA, who also saw it before it shot straight up.

title: Paulding Light
place: Robbins Pond Road, near Paulding, Michigan
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: In May 2010 students from the optics society (SPIE) chapter at Michigan Technological University watched the light through a telescope, saw that it was a pair of car headlights, and recreated it on cue by having one of them drive U.S. 45, about 4.5 miles away, with his hazard lights on.
shape: A light that brightens, dims, changes colour and seems to sway
witnesses: Visitors to the viewing spot, nightly since the 1960s
summary: From the end of Robbins Pond Road in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, visitors look north along a power-line cut and see a light rise, brighten, change colour and seem to sway before going out. Teenagers first reported it in 1966, and legends grew around it, the best known being the lantern of a railway brakeman killed on the line. In 2010 a group of Michigan Tech students set up a telescope at the spot and could make out pairs of headlights, then recreated the light on cue with a car on U.S. 45, the highway that crosses the line of sight about 4.5 miles away.

title: The lead masks of Vintém Hill
place: Morro do Vintém, Niterói, Rio de Janeiro
explanation: The likeliest account is an accidental overdose during an attempt at contact: a friend said the men were “scientific spiritualists”, their notebook told them to take capsules and wait for a signal, and mask-making materials were found at their homes. No toxicology was ever done, so the cause of death is officially unknown.
shape: A round orange light rising and falling over the hill (one resident’s report)
witnesses: A boy who found the bodies; police; a local resident who reported an orange light
summary: On August 17, 1966, two electronics technicians from Campos dos Goytacazes, Manoel Pereira da Cruz and Miguel José Viana, travelled to Niterói, bought raincoats and a bottle of water, and were last seen in a bar, one of them nervously checking his watch. On August 20 a boy flying a kite on Morro do Vintém found their bodies side by side, dressed in suits and raincoats, with crude lead eye-masks beside them. There were no signs of violence. A notebook held the instructions “16:30 be at the specified place. 18:30 swallow capsules, after the effect protect metals, await signal, mask”. The autopsy came weeks late and no toxicology was done, so the cause of death was never established. Days after the discovery, Rio newspapers reported that a resident had seen a round orange object rising and falling over the hill on the night the men went up, and the case entered UFO literature through Flying Saucer Review in 1967. There is no evidence linking the light to the deaths; a friend told police the men belonged to a group of “scientific spiritualists” who tried to contact other beings, which points to drugs taken in a ritual.

title: Malmstrom AFB Echo Flight shutdown
place: Echo Flight, Malmstrom AFB missile field, Montana
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The 1967 Air Force report found no UFO link and rumours "disproven". A 2025 Pentagon report stated the shutdown was caused by a classified electromagnetic-pulse test. Later accounts by former officers (Robert Salas) described a red glowing object over the gate.
shape: Reported glowing red object (1990s testimony)
witnesses: Launch crew; security guards (later testimony)
summary: All ten Minuteman I missiles of Echo Flight dropped off strategic alert almost simultaneously. Decades later, former missile officers said guards had reported a glowing red object hovering at the gate. The Air Force’s contemporaneous report found no UFO involvement.

title: Falcon Lake incident
place: Falcon Lake, Whiteshell Provincial Park, Manitoba
explanation: RCMP, RCAF and the Condon Committee could not explain it; some soil samples were mildly radioactive, possibly from radium paint. Later marks on Michalak’s body were judged self-inflicted.
shape: Two glowing oval objects; one landed
witnesses: Stefan Michalak
summary: Amateur prospector Stefan Michalak said two glowing craft descended near him; one landed on a rock outcrop. When he touched it, a blast of hot gas from a grid-like vent burned his chest. CBC has called it Canada’s best-documented UFO case.

title: UMMO — the San José de Valderas photographs
place: San José de Valderas, Alcorcón, near Madrid
explanation: A hoax. José Luis Jordán Peña, the main witness of the 1966 Aluche “landing”, admitted in the 1990s that he had invented UMMO as an experiment in credulity and that the photographs showed a small model hung from nylon thread; a stylistic study of the letters signed “Antonio Pardo” pointed to him, and in 1996 Manuel Carballal reproduced the pictures with a model on a fishing line.
shape: A circular craft with the UMMO sign, )+(, on its underside
witnesses: Anonymous photographers (“Antonio Pardo”); no credible eyewitnesses were found
duration: A few minutes, according to the photographers
summary: In June 1967 photographs of a round craft marked underneath with the sign )+( reached the Madrid newspaper Informaciones and Spanish UFO researchers, left anonymously at a photo shop in Carabanchel and sent by a man signing himself “Antonio Pardo”. They were said to have been taken on June 1 at San José de Valderas, outside Madrid. The sign was that of UMMO, a planet whose inhabitants had been writing long typed letters to Spanish enthusiasts since the mid-1960s, and the pictures made UMMO famous. No reliable witness of the flight was ever found; the negatives that were later analysed had gaps in their sequence, and a police laboratory study in the 1990s, while finding no thread, noted lighting that suggested artificial light and could not rule out fraud. In the 1990s José Luis Jordán Peña, a Madrid engineer with an interest in parapsychology, admitted that he had created UMMO, that he had written the letters with the help of a few friends, and that the photographs showed a model hung from a thread. Believers still defend the case.

title: Cussac — two children and four small black beings
explanation: No explanation has been agreed. The two children, aged 13 and 9, gave the same account to the police, and the police recorded a smell of sulphur and dried grass where the sphere was said to have stood. There were no other witnesses.
shape: Round craft about 4.6 m across, with four small black beings
witnesses: François (13) and his sister Anne-Marie (9)
summary: On August 29, 1967 a 13-year-old boy, François, and his 9-year-old sister, Anne-Marie, told the local police that while watching cows in a field at Cussac they had seen four small black beings, about 120 cm tall, with a shiny, silk-like look. The beings seemed to rise in the air and enter a round craft about 4.6 metres across that hovered over the field. The police noted a smell of sulphur and dried grass at the spot the craft was said to have left. The file is one of those that the French government put online in March 2007, and one of the children was later said to have suffered lasting health effects.

title: Six “flying saucers” across southern England (hoax)
place: A line of six sites from the Isle of Sheppey, Kent, to Clevedon, Somerset
explanation: A Rag Week hoax by aircraft engineering apprentices at the Royal Aircraft Establishment, Farnborough, led by Christopher Southall and Roger Palmer: fibreglass shells with an oscillator and loudspeaker inside, filled with fermenting flour paste. They owned up the same day and raised money for charity.
shape: Smooth, metallic-looking saucers about 1.4 m long, emitting a bleeping noise
witnesses: Members of the public who found them; four police forces, army bomb-disposal teams, the RAF and the MoD
summary: On the morning of Monday, September 4, 1967, people in southern England began finding small “flying saucers”, six in all, set out along a nearly straight line at about 51.5° N: on a housing estate near Queenborough on the Isle of Sheppey, on a golf course in Bromley, in a paddock at Winkfield near Ascot, at Welford near Newbury, at Chippenham, and on Dial Hill at Clevedon. Each was about 1.4 m long, weighed about 45 kg and gave out an eerie electronic sound. Police cordoned them off; army bomb-disposal teams, RAF helicopters and the Ministry of Defence’s intelligence staff were called in; the army blew up the Chippenham saucer, one was lifted from Sheppey by helicopter, and one was sent to the Atomic Weapons Research Establishment at Aldermaston. When one was drilled into, a foul-smelling paste burst out over the police. By the evening the makers, apprentices from the Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough, had owned up: it was a stunt for their Rag Week. The MoD’s file on the day was released by The National Archives.

title: Shag Harbour crash-landing
explanation: The RCMP, Canadian Coast Guard and Navy divers found no aircraft; the Condon Committee listed it as unexplained. No debris was recovered beyond a yellowish foam on the water.
shape: Row of 4 orange lights; object floating on the sea
witnesses: RCMP officers, fishermen, residents
summary: Residents and three RCMP officers watched orange lights descend at an angle and hit the water off Shag Harbour. Rescue boats found a patch of yellow foam but no aircraft; no plane was missing. Earlier that evening an Air Canada crew and a fishing boat’s radar also reported unusual objects.

title: Devon "flying cross" police chase
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The Ministry attributed it to the planet Venus, as it did several similar sightings that month.
shape: Star-spangled cross of light
witnesses: PCs Roger Willey and Clifford Waycott; a motorist; two BBC engineers
summary: Two police constables driving from Holsworthy to Hatherleigh saw a bright, cross-shaped light at treetop height. They followed it for about 14 miles, at up to 80 mph, and said it was like "looking through wet glass". A second object joined it at 04:23. A Land Rover driver saw it too. It faded at about 5 a.m. The case was raised in Parliament during the autumn 1967 "flying cross" wave.

title: Zond IV re-entry — the “craft with windows”
place: Across the sky from Kentucky through Ohio to Pennsylvania
explanation: NORAD identified the objects as fragments of the Soviet Zond IV probe or its rocket re-entering the atmosphere; Blue Book closed the case as satellite decay. The Condon study used it as its standard example of how honest witnesses turn a re-entry into a structured craft.
shape: Two or three fiery objects with golden-orange tails; some witnesses described a cigar-shaped craft with lit windows
witnesses: Hundreds of people along a line from Kentucky to Pennsylvania; about 78 written reports
summary: At about 9:45 p.m. EST on March 3, 1968, hundreds of people along a line from Kentucky to Pennsylvania saw a slow procession of fiery objects with golden-orange tails cross the sky to the north-east. Most saw two or three main pieces; some described a single long, wingless craft, said that “many windows seemed to be lit up from the inside”, or put it at treetop level. NORAD identified the objects as pieces of the Soviet Zond IV probe, launched on March 2, or of its rocket, and Project Blue Book recorded “satellite decay”; a contractor even estimated where surviving pieces might have fallen in north-central Pennsylvania. For the Condon study, William Hartmann compared about 30 detailed reports with the known event: many put the objects within a few miles and below 10,000 ft, when the debris was burning up tens of kilometres high, and the joining of separate lights into one windowed hull became his textbook case of the “airship effect”.

title: Minot AFB — B-52 radar and missile-field sightings
place: Minot AFB and missile field, North Dakota
explanation: Blue Book's conclusion: ground sightings were probably the B-52 and the star Sirius; the radar contact and the B-52's temporary loss of UHF radio were "possibly plasma", similar to ball lightning; the crew's sighting could have been the star Vega or a light on the ground.
evidence: radar | military-witness | pilot-witness | photo | official-document | em-effects
shape: Large glowing orange object
witnesses: Missile maintenance and security teams; B-52 crew
summary: Before dawn, maintenance and security teams at several Minuteman sites reported a large glowing object. A B-52 returning to Minot was asked to look for it. Its radar navigator painted a target that stayed about a mile off the bomber, and radarscope photographs were taken. The UHF radio dropped out when the object was closest. After landing, the crew described a bright light near the ground. Blue Book closed it within weeks. It is one of the best-documented military cases in the files.

title: Jimmy Carter’s light at Leary, Georgia
place: Outside the Lions Club meeting, Leary, Georgia
explanation: Robert Sheaffer and Allan Hendry identified it as Venus, which was near its greatest brilliancy in the western sky that evening; a later analysis proposed a barium-cloud release from a rocket fired at Eglin AFB. Carter himself said he never thought it was an alien craft.
shape: A bright light, as bright as the Moon, changing from white to blue to red and back
witnesses: Jimmy Carter, then a Georgia state senator and Lions Club district governor, and about ten others
summary: At about 7:15 one evening in 1969, Jimmy Carter was waiting outside a school lunchroom in Leary, Georgia, to speak to the local Lions Club, when one of the men pointed out a light in the west, about 30 degrees above the horizon. Carter said it seemed to come closer, stopped beyond the pine trees, changed from white to blue, then red, then white, and then receded, after 10 to 12 minutes. As governor, in September 1973, he filled in a sighting report for the International UFO Bureau, dating it October 1969; the Lions Club’s own records show his Leary speech was on January 6, 1969, and the club had disbanded before October. Investigators in 1976 found that most of those present did not remember the event. On January 6, Venus was a brilliant evening star in the direction Carter gave, which is the accepted explanation; Carter said later that he took it for something unexplained, not for a spacecraft.

title: Fort Beaufort — police fire at an object
place: Braeside farm near Fort Beaufort, Eastern Cape
shape: Fireball that changed colour
witnesses: Farmer Bennie Smit, farmhands and police officers
summary: Farmer Bennie Smit said he, his workers and local police fired shots at a fireball-like object that changed colour as it hovered among the trees on his farm. The story went around the world. Rumours said the army investigated the site but no records were produced. The town's "UFO Bar" and hotel clippings kept the story alive.

title: Lake Cote aerial survey photograph
explanation: Taken by the government’s Instituto Geográfico Nacional mapping aircraft; the object was not noticed at the time. Analyses have not produced an accepted identification.
shape: Metallic disc over the lake
witnesses: None at the time (found on the negative)
summary: An Instituto Geográfico Nacional aerial-survey camera flying at about 10,000 ft photographed Lake Cote for mapping. One frame shows a disc-like object over the water that the crew never saw; the adjacent frames do not show it.

title: Delphos ring
explanation: No official body reached a conclusion. The soil results are the main physical evidence; sceptics note that the account rests on one family, and that fungi can leave rings of altered, water-repelling soil.
shape: Mushroom-shaped, with multicoloured lights
witnesses: Ronnie Johnson (16) and his parents
summary: While doing evening chores on his family’s farm near Delphos, 16-year-old Ronnie Johnson saw a mushroom-shaped object, lit in many colours, hovering about 25 yards away. His parents came out to a glowing ring on the ground where it had been. It was still visible the next day. Investigators found that the soil in the ring was dry beside damp ground and would not let water through, and that it held more calcium and soluble salts and was more acidic, with a white deposit of calcium oxalate. Both calcium oxalate and oxalic acid irritate skin and eyes, and Ronnie’s parents said touching the ring numbed their fingers. It is one of the classic UFO “landing trace” cases.

title: Pascagoula encounter
explanation: No physical evidence was found beyond the two men’s testimony. Sceptics see a hoax or a hallucination; the witnesses stuck to their story, including when they were secretly recorded at the sheriff’s office.
shape: Oval object with flashing blue lights
witnesses: Charles Hickson (45) and Calvin Parker (17)
summary: Charles Hickson and his young colleague Calvin Parker said that while fishing from a pier on the west bank of the Pascagoula River they heard a whirring noise, saw two flashing blue lights and an oval object about 30–40 feet across, and were taken aboard by three creatures with claw-like hands, examined and returned. They went to the Jackson County sheriff’s office around 11 p.m. Officers who suspected a prank left the two alone in a room with a hidden recorder; the men’s talk matched their story. The case set off a wave of 1973 reports along the Gulf Coast and made Hickson a long-time public speaker; Parker published his own account in 2018.

title: Coyne helicopter incident
explanation: The sceptic Philip Klass argued that the crew first saw a bright fireball of the Orionid meteor shower and then misjudged what followed. Investigators for CUFOS and others reject this: by their timeline the object was in view for several minutes, and a family on the ground reported lights too.
shape: Grey cigar-shaped body, red nose light, white tail light, green beam
witnesses: Four-man Army Reserve crew; a family on the ground
summary: An Army Reserve Bell UH-1H (tail number 68-15444) on its way from Columbus to Cleveland was cruising at 2,500 feet near Mansfield when the crew saw a red light closing on the helicopter from the east. Capt. Lawrence Coyne took the controls and began an emergency descent, expecting a collision. They then saw a cigar-shaped grey object hover over the helicopter, with a red light at the nose, a white light at the tail and a green beam that lit the cockpit. After it left, the crew found the helicopter at about 3,500 feet in a climb of 1,000 feet a minute, with the collective still fully down, and the compass spinning. The Army Reserve’s report is among the best-known official records of an aircrew encounter.

title: Berwyn Mountains "crash"
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: A small earthquake shook the area at the same moment that a bright fireball was seen across northern England and Wales. The lights on the hillside were most likely poachers' lamps. Investigators found no crash and no recovery.
shape: Glowing light on the hillside
witnesses: Villagers across the Dee valley; a nurse who drove up the mountain
summary: At 20:38 a loud bang and tremor shook villages around the Berwyn Mountains, and people saw lights on the hillside. A local nurse drove up and described a glowing sphere. Police searched and found nothing. The event was later retold as a UFO crash with a secret military recovery, sometimes called "the Welsh Roswell". Seismographs recorded an earthquake, and meteor observers logged a fireball at the same moment.

title: Coyame “crash” — Chihuahua
explanation: Historians say the reports were most likely prompted by the crash and military recovery of a Cessna used for drug smuggling. The radar story that circulates in UFO literature is known only from later retellings.
shape: Disc-shaped object (as told)
witnesses: Local residents (reported)
summary: According to ufologists, residents near Coyame, in the Chihuahuan desert, reported a mid-air collision between a UFO and a small aeroplane on August 25, 1974, followed by a military recovery and a cover-up. The best-known version says U.S. air-defence radar followed a fast, high object from the Gulf of Mexico until it vanished near Coyame, and that a light aircraft that had left El Paso collided with it. Historians point instead to the real 1974 crash and recovery of a Cessna that had been carrying drugs, which they believe gave rise to the story. It is sometimes called Mexico’s Roswell. The case is listed because it is so often cited, not because the account is documented.

title: Langenburg rings
shape: Five domed discs
witnesses: 1 (farmer Edwin Fuhr)
summary: Farmer Edwin Fuhr was swathing a rapeseed field when he saw five metallic, dome-shaped objects spinning just above the ground near a slough. He sat frozen for about 15 minutes until they rose silently in formation and left, trailing grey vapour. He said his swather would not restart. The RCMP found five rings of flattened, swirled crop matching his description, with no tracks leading in.

title: Billy Meier’s “beamship” photographs
place: Zürcher Oberland, around Hinwil, canton of Zürich
explanation: A hoax. Meier’s former wife said in 1997 that the “beamships” were models made from household objects such as dustbin lids and carpet tacks; Meier admitted to Gary Kinder that he had used models to “recreate scenes”; and photographs of two “Pleiadian” women turned out to show dancers from the Golddiggers troupe on The Dean Martin Show.
shape: Disc-shaped “beamships” with domes and rings
witnesses: Eduard “Billy” Meier alone; no independent witness of any contact
summary: Eduard “Billy” Meier, from the canton of Zürich, says that on January 28, 1975, he met Semjase, a woman from the Pleiades, beside her spacecraft, and that contacts which had begun in his childhood went on for years. From 1975 he produced hundreds of sharp colour photographs and some film of saucer-shaped “beamships” over the fields and woods of the Zürcher Oberland, later the basis of books, a following and the 1987 film Contact. Scientists, sceptics and most ufologists regard them as fraudulent. Investigators such as Kal Korff argued that models had been photographed close up or combined with landscapes; Meier’s former wife Kalliope said in 1997 that she had seen the models and that the stories were invented; Meier conceded that he had used models to re-create scenes; and pictures he presented as the aliens Asket and Nera were traced to performers on American television.

title: Loring Air Force Base intrusions
place: Loring Air Force Base, Limestone, Maine
explanation: The Air Force never identified the object; its messages from the base describe an unidentified, helicopter-like aircraft that evaded the ground sweep. No conventional aircraft was found.
shape: Low aircraft with a red light and a white strobe
witnesses: Security police, including S/Sgt Danny Lewis
duration: About 40 minutes the first night; repeated for days
summary: On the evening of October 27, 1975 a security patrol at Loring Air Force Base, a Strategic Air Command base that held nuclear weapons, saw an aircraft with a red light and a white strobe approaching the north perimeter at about 300 feet. The base was put on alert and a ground sweep began. Over the next 40 minutes the object came within 300 yards of the restricted weapons storage area at about 150 feet, moving in ways described as helicopter-like, and no one could get a fix on it before it left toward Grand Falls, New Brunswick. Similar reports came from the base, and from other bases, for more than a week; Air Force messages about them were released under the Freedom of Information Act.

title: Wurtsmith Air Force Base and the KC-135 chase
place: Wurtsmith Air Force Base, Oscoda, Michigan
explanation: The NORAD log called it a helicopter over the weapons storage area, but no helicopter was identified, and the tanker crew described an object that pulled away each time they closed on it. It is one of a series of intrusions at northern Strategic Air Command bases that autumn, including Loring and Malmstrom.
shape: One white light pointing down and two red lights at the rear
witnesses: Base security police and the six-man crew of a KC-135 tanker
summary: At about 10:10 p.m. on October 30, 1975, guards at Wurtsmith, a Strategic Air Command base on Lake Huron, saw an object with a white light pointing downward and two red lights at the rear. Minutes later security police reported an “unidentified helicopter” hovering low over the weapons storage area, and the base radar approach control picked up a target about 35 miles to the south-east. A KC-135 tanker flying nearby was asked to look. Its six-man crew, among them Maj. Frederick Pappas, saw lights and painted the object on their radar for about ten seconds, and followed it at about 2,000 feet north over Lake Huron and then south toward Saginaw Bay; each time they closed in it sped away, and Capt. Myron Taylor put its final speed at about 1,000 knots. Low on fuel, they broke off. The NORAD log recorded that the tanker “made both visual sighting and radar skin paint” and that contact was lost 25 nautical miles south-east over Lake Huron.

title: Travis Walton disappearance
place: Apache–Sitgreaves National Forest near Heber, Arizona
explanation: The crew passed some polygraph tests and Walton failed one. Philip Klass and Michael Shermer argued it was a hoax, with a motive: the crew was behind on a Forest Service contract, and an "act of God" could excuse the penalty. Walton maintains it happened.
shape: Glowing disc hovering over a clearing
witnesses: 7 (the logging crew)
summary: A seven-man logging crew led by Mike Rogers was driving out of the forest after sunset when they saw a glowing disc over a clearing. Travis Walton got out and walked toward it, and the crew said a beam of light knocked him to the ground. They drove off in panic. When they came back he was gone. Police searched for five days. Walton then called his sister from a phone booth in Heber, saying he had been taken aboard. His story became the 1993 film Fire in the Sky.

title: Malmstrom AFB — objects over the missile fields, November 1975
place: Malmstrom Air Force Base and its Minuteman missile fields, Montana
shape: Lights over the launch facilities; on radar, slow targets that sounded like a jet
witnesses: Missile-site security teams, Air Defense radar operators and F-106 crews
summary: In the first weeks of November 1975, after the intrusions at Loring and Wurtsmith, NORAD’s logs and messages record a run of reports from the Minuteman fields around Malmstrom AFB in Montana. Security teams at several launch facilities reported lights and objects; Malmstrom’s search and height-finder radars carried a target between about 9,000 and 15,600 ft moving at only seven knots; witnesses said it sounded like a jet, and the FAA said no jets were in the area. F-106 interceptors scrambled from Malmstrom could not make contact because of the darkness and the target’s low altitude. The NORAD messages, released under the Freedom of Information Act by 1979, give no explanation. Later accounts add a security alarm at launch facility K-7, a glowing disc “the size of a football field” and tampered warheads; those details come from interviews years afterwards, not from the released records.

title: CFS Falconbridge — the NORAD message from Ontario
place: 30 nautical miles south-south-west of Canadian Forces Station Falconbridge, near Sudbury, Ontario
explanation: No explanation was given. The sighting came in the autumn of 1975, when bases along the northern U.S. border were also reporting lights and radar targets. The radar fixed only a bearing and range; the height and the vertical climb are the observers’ estimates.
shape: A circular, brilliantly lit object with two black spots in the centre
witnesses: Four members of the station (a major, a captain, a corporal and a master corporal); many reports to the Ontario Provincial Police in Sudbury
summary: At 11:15 UTC (6:15 a.m. local) on November 11, 1975, personnel at CFS Falconbridge, a Pinetree Line radar station north-east of Sudbury, saw and tracked an object bearing 210 degrees magnetic, 30 nautical miles from the station. 22nd NORAD Region Headquarters passed the report to the National Research Council in Ottawa: a “circular object, brilliantly lighted with two black spots in the center”, moving straight up “at high speed from 42,000 ft. to 72,000 ft.” with no horizontal movement, for 14 minutes, under broken cloud. The major who was the prime witness took photographs but did not know if they would come out. The same observers saw a similar object bearing 270 degrees, too far away for detail, and the Ontario Provincial Police in Sudbury received many other reports. The station’s history adds that two F-106 interceptors were scrambled from Selfridge Air National Guard Base in Michigan and saw nothing.

title: Canary Islands sphere
explanation: Spanish researcher Ricardo Campo matched the 1976 sighting, and similar Canary Islands events of the period, to U.S. Navy submarine-launched Poseidon missile tests in the Atlantic, whose exhaust clouds glow in sunlight at high altitude. The Spanish Air Force report left it unexplained.
shape: Light rising from the sea, then a huge glowing sphere
witnesses: Several hundred, including the crew of the Spanish Navy corvette Atrevida
summary: The crew of the corvette Atrevida saw a light rise from the sea, then a vast, luminous sphere spread out in the sky. Hundreds of people across Tenerife, La Palma, La Gomera and Gran Canaria saw it. A doctor near Gáldar said he saw two tall figures inside a transparent sphere. The Spanish Air Force investigation was leaked in 1977 and officially declassified in 1994.

title: Tehran F-4 Phantom intercepts
explanation: A U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency report called it "an outstanding report" meeting all criteria for a valid study. Skeptic Philip Klass proposed Jupiter plus coincidental equipment failures.
shape: Brilliant flashing lights; object released a smaller one
witnesses: Controllers, two F-4 crews, a general, civilians
summary: After civilian reports of a bright object over Tehran’s Shemiran district, the Imperial Iranian Air Force scrambled two F-4 Phantoms from Shahrokhi AB. Both crews said their instruments and communications failed near the object; the second pilot, Maj. Parviz Jafari, reported a radar lock and that his weapons panel died as a smaller object came toward him.

title: The Moroccan coast “UFO” — a Soviet rocket part re-entering
place: Along the Atlantic coast of Morocco, from Agadir to Kenitra and inland to Meknes and Fez
explanation: In 2012 the satellite tracker Ted Molczan matched the time and track to the re-entry of a piece of a Soviet Molniya rocket (an ullage-motor assembly from the third stage that orbited Molniya 1-35 in July 1976), an object catalogued by U.S. space tracking. The State Department’s 1976 reply had already said the sightings “could conceivably be compatible with a meteor, or a decaying satellite”. The witnesses’ estimate of 1,000 m was far too low, as estimates of a re-entry’s height usually are.
shape: A silvery, luminous flattened ball or a large luminous tube, shedding bright sparks from the rear
witnesses: People in Agadir, Kalaa Sraghna, Essaouira, Casablanca, Rabat, Kenitra, Meknes and around Fez, including Maj. Mohamed Lissaoui of the Royal Gendarmerie
summary: Between 1 and 2 a.m. on September 19, 1976, the Royal Gendarmerie took calls from Agadir, Marrakech, Casablanca, Rabat, Kenitra and other towns describing the same thing: a silent, silvery, luminous object, disc-shaped to some and tube-shaped to others, moving slowly from south to north parallel to the Atlantic coast and giving off intermittent trails of bright sparks and fragments. Major Mohamed Lissaoui of the Gendarmerie saw it himself at about 1:15 a.m. on his way back from Kenitra, flying low and slowly “as if it were an aircraft preparing to land”. King Hassan II sent the Gendarmerie’s commander, Col. Housni Benslimane, to the U.S. embassy on September 23 to ask what the Americans knew; the defence attaché was shown witnesses’ drawings and cabled Washington. The State Department answered that it knew of no U.S. aircraft or satellite activity and that a meteor or a decaying satellite was possible. The cables became public through WikiLeaks in 2013.

title: Talavera la Real air base sentries
place: Talavera la Real Air Base, Badajoz
shape: Intense light; tall luminous figure
witnesses: 3 soldiers on guard duty
summary: Two soldiers on night patrol at Talavera la Real air base heard a sound like radio interference that became a piercing whistle. When it stopped they saw an intense light in the sky for about 15 seconds. With a third guard and a guard dog they searched the perimeter. The dog came back cowering, and they said they saw a tall, glowing figure and fired their rifles at it before it vanished. The Spanish Air Force investigated and later released its file.

title: Broad Haven schoolchildren — the Welsh Triangle
explanation: A Ministry of Defence investigator found no physical evidence that anything had landed and suggested that “a local prankster” might have been responsible. The children’s drawings agreed closely, which is why the case is still told.
shape: Yellow cigar-shaped craft; later an “upside-down saucer”
witnesses: 14 schoolchildren, then teachers and a hotel owner
duration: Lunchtime on Feb 4; further reports to April
summary: At lunchtime on February 4, 1977 a group of 14 children at Broad Haven Primary School reported a yellow, cigar-shaped craft that landed in a field beyond the school grounds, and a silver creature with pointed ears. The headmaster had them draw what they saw, and the drawings agreed closely. On February 17 teachers and others said they saw the same craft, and on April 19 the owner of the Haven Fort Hotel in nearby Little Haven reported an “upside-down saucer” and two figures in a field. The wave of sightings in the area became known as the Dyfed or Welsh Triangle. A Ministry of Defence investigator found nothing to show a landing. The events were revisited in a 2023 Netflix documentary and a 2024 BBC series.

title: Corporal Valdés — the patrol at Pampa Lluscuma
explanation: Valdés himself said in later interviews (reported for 2004, 2009 and 2013) that it was a joke among the patrol that got out of hand, with the watch set forward and the beard explained away to avoid punishment for not shaving, though at other times he has said it happened. The army never investigated and the watch was never examined.
shape: Bright violet lights descending from the sky
witnesses: Corporal Armando Valdés Garrido and seven conscripts of a Chilean Army patrol
summary: In the early hours of April 25, 1977, a Chilean Army patrol of a corporal and seven conscripts camped on the Pampa Lluscuma, in the altiplano near Putre, said two bright lights came down near them. Corporal Armando Valdés walked towards one and disappeared; about fifteen minutes later he came back, collapsed and said, “You don’t know who we are or where we come from, but I assure you we will return.” The soldiers said his face now carried several days’ beard and his digital watch showed a date five days ahead. The story reached the press across the world, from Chilean papers to French ones, and became Chile’s best-known UFO case. It was never investigated under the military government: no statement was taken officially and the watch was neither photographed nor studied. Later reporting found that the group was guarding army horses rather than patrolling, and some soldiers said Valdés had a beard before that night. Valdés has given contradictory accounts since, at times calling it a prank that got out of hand.

title: Petrozavodsk phenomenon
explanation: Usually attributed to the launch of Kosmos-955 from Plesetsk, but the 1977 Academy of Sciences report said the phenomenon could not be satisfactorily understood.
shape: Glowing "jellyfish" showering rays
witnesses: Thousands, from Helsinki to Vladivostok
summary: In the early hours, residents of Petrozavodsk saw a glowing object spread over the city like a jellyfish, "raining" shafts of light. Reports came from across the Soviet Union and Finland. The event prompted the Soviet research programme Setka.

title: Colares "chupa-chupa" & Operação Prato
explanation: The Brazilian Air Force closed Operação Prato after about four months, reporting no unusual phenomena; its files and photos are in the Arquivo Nacional.
shape: Beams of light, "chupa-chupa" lights
witnesses: Islanders; Brazilian Air Force team
summary: Residents of Colares reported lights that fired beams and left burn-like marks. The mayor asked for help, and the Brazilian Air Force ran Operação Prato under Capt. Uyrangê Hollanda, photographing lights over several months. Hollanda gave a dramatic interview two decades later.

title: The object that fell near Bermejo — Bolivia’s 1978 search
place: El Taire hill above the Bermejo River, Tarija department, on the Argentine border
shape: A luminous cylinder or egg with a flaming tail
witnesses: Many people along the border; Bolivian Air Force pilots who searched the slope
duration: Seconds (the fall), followed by an explosion
summary: In the afternoon of May 6, 1978 (some reports say the Sunday evening, May 7), people on both sides of the Bermejo River, where Bolivia’s Tarija department meets Argentina, saw a luminous object with a fiery tail fall towards the El Taire hill and heard an explosion and a sonic boom. The Bolivian army and police searched, scientists from the University of Tarija went to the area, Argentina sent border police, and newspapers in Buenos Aires carried a police chief’s description of a dull metal cylinder about four metres long. The U.S. Embassy in La Paz reported the fall to Washington, and two U.S. Air Force attachés flew to Tarija; the embassy denied any secret recovery. A CIA-released bulletin of May 17, 1978 is headed “Bolivia reports conflict on details of fallen object”. The searches, slowed by the terrain and weather, recovered nothing anyone published. Explanations at the time ranged from a meteorite to space debris; no country reported losing a satellite, no meteorite fall is catalogued there for that date, and the object was never identified.

title: Emilcin abduction report
shape: White, hovering, humming craft
witnesses: 1 (farmer Jan Wolski)
summary: Jan Wolski, a 71-year-old farmer, said that while driving his horse-drawn cart through the woods near Emilcin, two short beings with greenish faces invited him aboard a white craft hovering over a clearing. There they examined him. He was later interviewed by investigators, who found him sincere. A monument now stands near the site, one of the few UFO memorials in the world.

title: Gujan-Mestras — the light that put out the street lamps
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: GEIPAN class B: the witnesses probably saw an atmospheric phenomenon linked to the thunderstorm threatening the area. The gendarmerie and GEPAN could not link the town sighting to a light seen by motorists near La Réole.
shape: An orange, oval luminous object
witnesses: Several residents; motorists on the RN113 near La Réole
summary: On the night of June 19, 1978, several people in Gujan-Mestras, on the Arcachon basin, heard a loud, dull noise and then saw an orange, oval light over the town. While it was there the street lighting faltered; the light faded from view as it climbed. Motorists on the road to Bordeaux near La Réole also saw a light moving slowly in the stormy sky. The gendarmerie took statements and GEPAN, the French space agency’s UFO office, investigated. GEIPAN classes the case B: probably a weather phenomenon connected with the storm. The two sightings could not be shown to be the same thing.

title: Disappearance of Frederick Valentich
place: Bass Strait, off Cape Otway, Victoria
explanation: The Department of Transport could not determine the cause. Theories include disorientation (seeing his own lights reflected while inverted), a staged disappearance and suicide.
shape: "Long shape" with four bright lights, orbiting above
witnesses: Pilot (radio transcript); later ground reports
summary: Twenty-year-old Frederick Valentich, flying a Cessna 182L from Moorabbin to King Island, told Melbourne Flight Service a large lit aircraft was orbiting over him. His last words were "It is not an aircraft", followed by 17 seconds of metallic noise. No trace of him or the aircraft was ever found.

title: Clarenville — RCMP constable watches object over the water
shape: Oval with a fin, lights
witnesses: 12, including RCMP Constable James Blackwood
summary: In the early morning a dozen people in Clarenville called the RCMP about an object hovering over the water toward Random Island. Constable James Blackwood watched it for one to two hours through a surveillance telescope. He described an oval with a fin at the back, hanging about 100 ft above the water. When he flashed his headlights, the object seemed to flash back. It then vanished and left no trace.

title: Kuwait’s oil-field sightings and the pumps that stopped
place: Kuwait Oil Company fields around Umm al-Aish, near the satellite earth station, northern Kuwait
explanation: The government’s committee of experts from the Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research ruled out spy aircraft but gave no explanation, and its report was never published. The U.S. embassy reported the stop and restart of the pumping equipment as a Kuwait Oil Company official described it; nothing else about the landing is documented beyond press accounts.
shape: A dazzling light; close up, a domed disc the size of a jumbo jet with a red light on top
witnesses: Staff of a Kuwait Oil Company pumping station, including an American, and of the nearby satellite station
duration: About seven minutes on the ground; the series of sightings ran for five weeks
summary: On the night of November 9–10, 1978, according to the Kuwaiti dailies Al-Qabas and Al-Watan, employees of the Kuwait Oil Company and of the satellite station near Umm al-Aish saw a dazzling light come down nearby. Four oil-company workers, one of them an American, went to within about 250 metres and saw a disc as big as a jumbo jet, with a cupola and a red light on top, which stayed on the ground for about seven minutes while telephone and radio links in the area were cut, then rose vertically at great speed. Sightings over the oil fields went on until December 14. The U.S. embassy’s cable to Washington in January 1979, “UFO sightings cause security concern in Kuwait”, reported that the government had set up a committee of experts from the Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research, and that a senior Kuwait Oil Company official said the oil-pumping equipment had shut down automatically during one sighting and started again by itself when the object left, although it could normally be restarted only by hand.

title: Zanfretta — the Torriglia night patrol
explanation: Sceptics say the grass imprint matched the place where the owners tied a horse, that regression hypnosis can create false memories, that the beings resembled characters in popular 1978 Italian TV and comics, and that the “footprints” were puddles. Italy’s national UFO centre (CUN) judged the case unreliable.
shape: Red oval craft over 10 m across; later a triangular craft
witnesses: Pier Fortunato Zanfretta (a security guard); 52 other statements
summary: At about 11:30 p.m. on December 6, 1978 the 26-year-old security guard Pier Fortunato Zanfretta, on patrol at Marzano, in the municipality of Torriglia, noticed four lights in the garden of a mansion called Casa Nostra and then a red oval object more than ten metres across. He radioed his supervisor that “they are not men”, then contact was lost; he was found unconscious and in shock. He described three-metre beings with mottled skin, yellow triangular eyes and clawed feet. A semicircular imprint of flattened grass was found in the garden, and Carabinieri Brigadier Antonio Nucchi collected 52 statements from people who had seen strange lights that night. A neurologist found no mental disturbance in January 1979. Zanfretta later described further abductions, eleven in all between 1978 and 1981, which are the most disputed part of the story.

title: Kaikōura lights
explanation: Explanations offered include Venus and Jupiter, squid-fishing boat lights, and meteors; none accounts for the radar returns to everyone’s satisfaction.
shape: Bright white lights with a red tinge; pulsing orb
witnesses: Safe Air crew, TV crew, Wellington radar
summary: After a Safe Air crew reported lights tracked by Wellington radar on 21 December, an Australian TV crew rode along on the Argosy newspaper run. On the night of 30–31 December they filmed lights pacing the aircraft off the Kaikōura coast in colour on 16 mm film, with Wellington controllers reporting matching radar returns.

title: Cecconi G.91R photographs over Treviso
explanation: The Italian Defence Ministry later said its photo interpreters had identified the object as a cylindrical balloon made of black plastic bags (a "solar balloon"). Cecconi rejected this, noting the object did not move in his jet's wake.
shape: Dull black, capsule-shaped, with a milky dome
witnesses: Maresciallo Giancarlo Cecconi; Istrana radar; Treviso tower
summary: Returning from a photo-reconnaissance sortie in a G.91R, Italian Air Force pilot Giancarlo Cecconi was asked to identify an object tracked by Istrana radar over Treviso air base. He found a dull black, capsule-shaped object about 6–8 m long at about 1,300 m. He made passes within about 100 m and took more than 80 photographs with the aircraft's reconnaissance cameras. Then radar and the tower both lost it.

title: Pranles — the yellow light with a turning blue beam
shape: A stationary yellow-orange light projecting a blue beam that turned through 360°
witnesses: Two couples in neighbouring houses; the first witness a scientist who worked on light and colour
summary: From 22:45 to 23:28 on July 21, 1979, a couple at Pranles, in the Ardèche, watched a stationary yellow-orange light on top of a ridge towards the Serre de Pieroulet, like a lighthouse, projecting a blue beam that turned steadily through 360° and swept the ground. No sound was heard. As the husband, a scientist who worked on light and colour, prepared to take a photograph, it went out. Their neighbours had seen the same light in the same direction before closing their shutters at about 23:00. He reported it to the gendarmerie the next day. Re-examining the case decades later, GEIPAN found that a helicopter with a searchlight was the only plausible explanation, but a blue beam from a yellow source, turning continuously for no purpose, did not fit it. The case stays class D, unexplained, though GEIPAN notes it is near the line between unexplained and unusable because no field investigation was made at the time.

title: Val Johnson — deputy's patrol car struck by a light
explanation: UFO researchers (Allan Hendry, Jerome Clark) consider it significant. Skeptic Philip Klass argued it was a hoax and that Johnson damaged the car himself. The patrol car is on display at the Marshall County museum.
shape: Beam of bright light just above the road
witnesses: 1 (Deputy Sheriff Val Johnson)
summary: Deputy Val Johnson was patrolling rural roads when he saw a bright light just above the road. It rushed toward his car, the car was engulfed in light, and he heard glass breaking. He said he was unconscious for 39 minutes. Deputies found the car skewed across the road. The windshield was cracked, a headlight and the roof light were broken, and an aerial was bent. Both his watch and the car's clock were 14 minutes slow. A doctor compared his eye irritation to "welder's burns".

title: Dechmont Law — Robert Taylor
shape: Dome-shaped object; two spiked spheres
witnesses: 1 (forester Robert Taylor)
summary: Forestry worker Robert Taylor walked into a clearing on Dechmont Law and saw a large dome-shaped object hovering. He said two smaller spiked spheres rolled out, grabbed his trousers and dragged him toward it, and he passed out. He came to with torn trousers, grazes and a headache, and staggered home. Police recorded the case as an assault and found marks in the ground. It is often described as the only UFO event police have investigated as a crime. A marker now stands at the site.

title: Manises — airliner diversion & Mirage intercept
explanation: Spanish Air Force files declassified in the 1990s did not confirm an anomalous object; researchers attribute the lights to refinery flare stacks and bright stars/planets.
shape: Red lights on a collision course; truncated cone
witnesses: TAE crew, 109 passengers, controllers, Mirage pilot
summary: TAE flight JK-297 from Salzburg (via Palma) to Las Palmas saw red lights approach on a collision course near Ibiza and track the aircraft after it changed altitude. The captain diverted to Valencia — the first airliner diverted by a UFO. A Mirage F1 from Los Llanos then chased lights that accelerated away.

title: Cergy-Pontoise “abduction” (hoax)
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: A hoax. GEIPAN, which reviewed the police and gendarmerie inquiry and its own analyses, calls it “a hoax whose course discredits the scientific work”; one of the friends is reported to have admitted years later that he made the story up.
shape: A light over the road that wrapped the car in fog and small flashing spheres
witnesses: Three young men; the police and gendarmes arrived after the call
summary: Before dawn on November 26, 1979, a young man telephoned the police at Cergy-Pontoise to say his friend had been “abducted by a UFO”. Three friends said they had been loading jeans to sell at a market when a light appeared over the road; the driver went towards it, it wrapped the car in fog and small flashing spheres, and when the fog cleared he was gone. Seven police officers and gendarmes searched; the story became national news. The missing man reappeared at a friend’s flat on December 3, with a journalist present, saying he had woken in a cabbage field. GEPAN’s technical note found that the witnesses’ accounts diverged from the start, that a blood test gave no sign of time in weightlessness, and that cabbages said to have been dried by the light had been left to rot as fertiliser by their owner. GEIPAN classes the affair as a hoax.

title: La Joya air base pursuit
place: La Joya air base, Arequipa, Peru
explanation: Peru’s air force kept the case quiet for decades; no explanation has been published. Peru has since set up an office (now DIFAA) for aerial anomalies, and U.S. documents on the case were later released.
shape: Large balloon-shaped object
witnesses: Lt Oscar Santa María Huertas; some 1,800 people at the base
summary: On the morning of April 11, 1980 about 1,800 people at the La Joya base saw a large, balloon-shaped object hanging still at around 500 metres. Lt Oscar Santa María Huertas, 23, took off in a Sukhoi Su-22 and fired 64 rounds at it without effect. He reported that it climbed away at up to 950 km/h, reaching about 19,200 metres, and stopped so suddenly that he had to swerve to avoid it. Peruvian army radar was said to show only his aircraft, while operators saw the object by eye. The engagement is said to have lasted 22 minutes, until his fuel ran low. The Peruvian Air Force kept the matter classified for decades; U.S. defence documents titled “UFO sighted in Peru” have since been released.

title: Todmorden — PC Alan Godfrey
shape: Diamond-shaped object hovering over the road
witnesses: PC Alan Godfrey; other officers saw a light that night
summary: Before dawn, PC Alan Godfrey was driving his patrol car along Burnley Road looking for missing cattle when he found a large, diamond-shaped object hovering about 5 ft above the road, blocking it. He sketched it from the car. The next thing he knew, he was farther down the road and some time had passed. He said the road surface under the object was dry though the rest was wet. Other officers reported a light in the sky that night. Later hypnosis sessions produced an abduction account.

title: Rendlesham Forest
place: Rendlesham Forest, outside RAF Woodbridge, Suffolk
explanation: The Ministry of Defence found no threat and did not investigate further. Skeptics attribute the lights to a fireball, the Orford Ness lighthouse (visible through the trees in the same direction) and bright stars.
shape: Metallic lit object in the forest; star-like lights
witnesses: USAF security police; Lt. Col. Charles Halt
summary: USAF security patrols at the east gate of RAF Woodbridge saw lights descend into the forest and went in to investigate. Two nights later deputy base commander Lt. Col. Charles Halt led a team that took radiation readings at three ground depressions and recorded his observations on a micro-cassette. His memo to the MoD is one of the most famous UFO documents in Britain.

title: Cash–Landrum incident
explanation: Army and Air Force inquiries found no helicopters or craft that matched; the witnesses’ lawsuit against the U.S. government was dismissed in 1986. Skeptics question the medical and helicopter claims.
shape: Diamond-shaped object venting flame; escorted by ~23 helicopters
witnesses: Betty Cash, Vickie & Colby Landrum; other motorists
summary: Driving home through the pine woods north-east of Houston, Betty Cash and Vickie Landrum with her grandson said a blazing diamond-shaped object hovered over the road, radiating heat. As it rose, they counted about two dozen helicopters, many resembling CH-47 Chinooks. All three reported injuries afterwards, and they sued the U.S. government.

title: Trans-en-Provence landing trace
explanation: The French government’s GEPAN (now GEIPAN, part of CNES) analysed soil and plant samples and reported heating and biochemical changes it could not attribute to a known cause. Skeptics suggest a vehicle or the witness.
shape: Lead-grey disc, two stacked saucers
witnesses: Renato Nicolaï
summary: Renato Nicolaï heard a whistle and saw an object land briefly on his terrace and fly off. The Gendarmerie took samples within a day; GEPAN’s laboratory analysis of the 2.4 m circular mark reported soil heated to 300–600 °C and chlorophyll changes in alfalfa leaves.

title: The spiral over south-west China
place: Sichuan and Yunnan, and across south-west, north-west and south-central China
explanation: Newspapers first quoted astronomers blaming a meteor shower; the astronomer Liu Yan of the Purple Mountain Observatory, who analysed the eyewitness reports, concluded it was a man-made object about 650 km up, and an article in the space magazine Hangtian put it at about 500 km and rejected the meteor idea. A slowly turning spiral of light seen from half a country is what a rocket stage venting propellant in sunlight looks like (compare the Norwegian and Australian spirals), but no launch has been matched to this one.
shape: A star-like point that brightened and grew a spinning, silver, spiral-shaped band of light
witnesses: Very many people across several provinces; the Hangtian article claims ten million
summary: At 10:38 p.m. on July 24, 1981, on a clear, moonless night, people across Sichuan, Yunnan, Gansu and neighbouring provinces saw a bright, star-like point grow brighter, begin to oscillate and develop a cloud-like band of light that turned into a huge silver spiral, spinning as it crossed the sky slowly from east to west. It was in view for six or seven minutes. The sighting started a nationwide craze for UFOs in the newly opened China; the U.S. Air Force’s Foreign Technology Division translated a Hangtian article about it, “UFO incident causes sensation throughout half of China”, which weighed a meteor, an aircraft and a flying saucer. Liu Yan, the Purple Mountain Observatory astronomer who handled many of the letters the public sent about UFOs in the 1980s, made it the subject of his first article on them and concluded it was man-made.

title: Hannah McRoberts’ photograph — Vancouver Island
place: A provincial park by the Eve River bridge on Highway 19, near Kelsey Bay, Vancouver Island, British Columbia
explanation: The NASA scientist Richard Haines examined the negative in 1987 and found no sign of tampering or a support thread; his measurements put the disc at least 30 feet from the camera, and interviews and a site survey supported the family’s account. Because nobody saw the object, a thrown object (a Frisbee, a hubcap or a pan lid have been suggested) cannot be ruled out, and later re-analyses from prints rather than the negative leave the case open.
shape: A sharply focused, domed disc against clear blue sky above a mountain peak
witnesses: None saw the object; the photographer, Hannah McRoberts, her husband and daughter were present
duration: One frame of 35 mm colour film
summary: At about 11 a.m. on October 8, 1981, Hannah McRoberts photographed a mountain peak from a provincial park off Highway 19 near Kelsey Bay, on the north-east coast of Vancouver Island, while travelling with her husband and young daughter. Nobody noticed anything in the sky. When the film was developed days later, one frame showed a sharply focused, dark, domed disc above the peak. Richard Haines, a perception scientist at NASA Ames, examined the original negative with micro-densitometry and computer enhancement, visited the site and interviewed the family; he found no evidence of a hoax, concluded the object was three-dimensional and at least 30 feet away, and presented the photograph to the 1997 Sturrock panel on UFO evidence. It is still one of the most reproduced UFO photographs, and one of the most argued over.

title: Brest-Guipavas airport — the fireball by the runway
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: GEIPAN class B: probably a meteoroid entering the atmosphere on a shallow path, seen nearly head-on, which explains the red-orange ball, the short, slow descent and the sudden disappearance. A radar “spot” first cited in the file was not supported: the controllers noted nothing abnormal.
shape: A red-orange ball, low on the horizon, that seemed to drop into a field by the runway
witnesses: Seven people in four independent groups: joggers, airport firefighters and a man waiting for a bus
duration: Seconds (15 s or less, by most accounts)
summary: At about 7:55 on the morning of November 22, 1981, in early light, people in four separate groups near Brest-Guipavas airport saw a red-orange ball low over the horizon that seemed to fall into a field beside a runway and vanish; some saw sparks or a short trail. The airport’s firefighters, who watched it come down as if landing, alerted the control tower. The gendarmes, contacted the next day by the air traffic controller, took eight statements and searched; no trace was found. GEPAN’s original file recorded a radar echo at the time, which made the case a class D, unexplained. GEIPAN’s re-examination found that the radar centre had treated the echoes as insignificant and that the controllers had seen nothing abnormal, and reclassified it B: a meteoroid on a grazing path, seen almost head-on.

title: Trancrainville — gendarmes on the A10 and the lit-up ground
place: A10 motorway near Trancrainville, Eure-et-Loir, north of Orléans
shape: An indistinct bright mass in the sky, and a strongly lit patch on the ground
witnesses: Two gendarmes of the motorway patrol
summary: Between 4:35 and 4:55 a.m. on January 23, 1982, two gendarmes of the motorway patrol, driving south on the A10, saw an indistinct bright mass in the sky and a strongly lit area on the ground beneath it, which moved across pylons and hangars. They followed it for about 30 km, driving and stopping, losing and finding it again, and heard nothing even with the engine off; at the end only a glow remained to the east over the trees. The Orléans air base, 7 km away, had nothing flying and its radar had been off since the evening before, and the motorway operator’s staff had seen nothing. Re-examining the case, GEIPAN rejected planets (they cannot light the ground) and judged a helicopter with a searchlight above the cloud, then at 1,200–1,500 m, too unlikely for the equipment of the time. It is class D, unexplained, with the caveat that no field interview could be made.

title: VASP flight 169 — the light that paced a Boeing 727
place: Night flight from Fortaleza to Rio de Janeiro, first seen near Petrolina, Pernambuco
explanation: A study in the Journal of Scientific Exploration (2014) concluded the light was the planet Venus, rising brilliantly before dawn and possibly distorted by an atmospheric mirage. The captain rejected that, saying he knew Venus and the Moon; a radar return the air-traffic centre reported near the airliner has never been documented in detail.
shape: A bright light changing from red to orange, with a white and bluish centre
witnesses: Captain Gérson Maciel de Britto, his co-pilot and many passengers; crews of two other airliners
summary: VASP’s night flight 169, a Boeing 727 (PP-SNG) under Captain Gérson Maciel de Britto, left Fortaleza at 01:50 on February 8, 1982 for Rio de Janeiro. About half an hour later, near Petrolina, the captain saw a light approach on the left and pace the aircraft. It changed colour between red and orange around a white and bluish centre, seemed to move above and below the airliner, and stayed with it past Belo Horizonte; at 31,000 ft the crew said a bluish light filled the cabin. Britto called the air-traffic and air-defence centre CINDACTA in Brasília, which had no traffic there, dimmed his lights and flashed his landing lights at it, and woke the passengers; one compared it to a mercury street lamp. CINDACTA later said its radar showed a return about eight miles from the aircraft, and crews of a Transbrasil and an Aerolíneas Argentinas flight reported seeing something. The light was lost in cloud over the Serra do Mar a few minutes before landing at Galeão. The case was examined in the Journal of Scientific Exploration in 2014, which concluded that the “object” was Venus, very bright in the eastern pre-dawn sky.

title: Morenão stadium sighting
